summary: Describes Bidirectional PIM, a variant of PIM Sparse-Mode that builds bidirectional shared trees for multicast. A Designated Forwarder election on each link lets data flow to the Rendezvous Point and receivers without source-specific state. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: BIDIR-PIM carries multicast traffic toward and away from a shared tree root. It elects one router on each link to forward that traffic, allowing routers to use shared tree information instead of keeping state for each source.

subtitle: Bidirectional multicast trees use one elected forwarder per link and rendezvous-point address.

tldr.problem: PIM Sparse-Mode can send source traffic to a Rendezvous Point by encapsulating it or building source-specific state. The RFC describes the processing, bandwidth, delay, protocol and memory costs of these approaches.
tldr.mechanism: BIDIR-PIM elects a Designated Forwarder for each Rendezvous Point Address on each link except the Rendezvous Point Link. That router forwards traffic upstream and downstream using shared tree state.
tldr.outcome: BIDIR-PIM avoids source-specific state and data-driven protocol events for this forwarding method. RFC 5015 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

today: RFC 5015 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

sections.title: Why Use Bidirectional Shared Trees
sections.content:
Bidirectional Protocol Independent Multicast (BIDIR-PIM) is a variant of PIM Sparse-Mode that connects multicast sources and receivers through a shared tree. Each tree has a Rendezvous Point (RP) as its root.

In ordinary PIM Sparse-Mode, a source's first-hop router can encapsulate its packets in Register messages to the RP. Another option builds source-specific state along the path between the source and the RP. The RFC identifies processing, bandwidth and delay costs for encapsulation, and protocol and memory costs for source-specific state.

BIDIR-PIM instead forwards source packets toward the RP using shared tree state. Its forwarding does not require source-specific state or data-driven protocol events.
sections.plainLanguage: BIDIR-PIM uses one shared multicast tree for traffic traveling toward and away from its root. Routers do not need to create separate forwarding state for each source.

sections.title: The Root, Link and Designated Forwarder
sections.content:
A Rendezvous Point Address (RPA) is the root address for a range of multicast groups. It must be routable throughout the PIM domain, but it does not need to belong to an interface on a real router. The Rendezvous Point Link (RPL) is the physical link to which that address belongs; no Designated Forwarder election takes place on the RPL.

On every other link, one Designated Forwarder (DF) per RPA handles forwarding for the groups assigned to that RPA. The DF is selected using routing metrics from the Multicast Routing Information Base. It forwards downstream traffic onto its link and picks up upstream traffic from the link toward the RPL.

Upstream means toward the RPA, and downstream means away from it. The DF also processes Join messages and forwards packets to local receivers learned through a membership mechanism such as IGMP or MLD.
sections.plainLanguage: The RPA is the address at the root of a set of multicast trees. Each other link has one elected router that forwards traffic between the link and that root.

sections.title: Forwarding Traffic in Both Directions
sections.content:
A packet for a multicast group is accepted when it arrives on the router's interface toward the RPA, or when the router is DF on the incoming interface. The router builds the outgoing interface list for that group, removes the incoming interface from the list and forwards the packet on any remaining interfaces.

The DF is the only router on its link that forwards downstream packets onto that link or accepts upstream packets from it for forwarding toward the RPL. Other routers can forward downstream packets from the RPF interface to receivers, and can pass a source's traffic onto a link where they are the DF.

A branch used only by sources and with no receivers needs no group-specific state. It can use the RPA-specific information alone. An implementation may keep group state there for accounting or performance, but then it needs data-driven events to discover active groups.
sections.plainLanguage: A router forwards a packet only when it arrives from the root-facing interface or from a link where that router is the elected forwarder. It then sends the packet on the group's other relevant interfaces.

sections.title: Building the Tree with Join and Prune
sections.content:
A last-hop router that is DF on a link with receivers sends a group Join toward the RPA. The Join travels hop by hop until it reaches a router connected to the RPL. These Joins build the group-specific distribution tree between receivers and the root link.

For each group and interface, a router tracks whether it has no Join state, Join state, or PrunePending state. A received Join starts or refreshes an expiry timer. A Prune starts a short timer so another downstream router can override it; when that timer expires, forwarding stops and the router may send a PruneEcho to itself for reliability.

Upstream, the router tracks whether it is joined to the tree. It sends periodic Joins while downstream receivers need the group, suppresses its Join if another router has already sent one to the same upstream neighbor, and sends a Prune when the group is no longer needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A router with interested receivers asks the next router toward the RPA to keep the group connected. When no downstream router needs the group, a Prune can remove that branch.

sections.title: Electing and Replacing a Forwarder
sections.content:
The DF election is held once per RPA on each link, so groups that share an RPA also share the election result. Routers compare their unicast routing metrics to the RPA. A router whose route to the RPA uses the link being considered advertises an infinite metric because it cannot forward traffic from that link toward the RPL.

Routers exchange Offer messages with their metrics. A router that sends its offer the Election_Robustness number of times without hearing a better offer sends Winner and becomes DF. If an acting DF receives a better offer, it sends Backoff and then Passes responsibility to the best offering router. The old DF stops when it sends Pass; the new DF takes over when it receives Pass.

The procedure favors suspending forwarding and discarding uncertain DF information rather than risk two routers forwarding on one link. This reduces the possibility of forwarding loops. The RFC describes optional reliability measures, including detecting a missing Pass and repeating Winner announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers compare their routes to the RPA and elect one forwarder for the link. If a router with a better route appears, the current forwarder sends a Pass so the new one can take over.

sections.title: Election Messages and Default Timers
sections.content:
PIM control messages use IP protocol number 103. BIDIR-PIM election messages use PIM version 2 and Type 10, and are sent with TTL 1 to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group: 224.0.0.13 for IPv4 or ff02::d for IPv6.

The message subtypes are Offer (1), Winner (2), Backoff (3) and Pass (4). A Backoff message includes the offering router's address and metric plus a wait interval. A Pass message identifies the new winner and its metric. BIDIR-PIM routers also include the Bidirectional Capable Hello option, OptionType 22, in their Hello messages.

The default Offer_Period is 100 milliseconds, the Backoff_Period is 1 second and Election_Robustness is 3. The default periodic Join/Prune interval is 60 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The election uses four numbered message types to compare routes and transfer the forwarding role. A Hello option tells neighboring routers that this router supports BIDIR-PIM.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BIDIR-PIM messages are link-local multicast messages, so an attack requires a directly connected node or the cooperation of one. Forged election messages can make the wrong router appear to be DF or prevent an election from converging.

The RFC recommends authenticating election-message sources. When authentication is available, routers MUST discard spoofed messages and SHOULD log a rate-limited warning. Routers SHOULD also check the destination Ethernet address of election messages, though this does not work on links without layer-2 multicast delivery.

The RFC recommends IPsec transport mode with the Authentication Header for authentication. Routers SHOULD limit which neighbors can send Join/Prune, Assert and election messages, and SHOULD NOT accept messages from a router before receiving its valid Hello.
sections.plainLanguage: A nearby device could send false election messages and disrupt forwarding. Authentication and limits on accepted neighbors help routers reject messages from unauthorized sources.
